title: Use AI Tools
subtitle: Claude, ChatGPT & friends — for real work
description: A Teachy how-to-use path: open a real AI tool, write clear prompts, get something usable, fix weak output, and explain what you did. AI fluency is Teachy itself — this is one tool path among many (websites, agents, Wispr Flow, etc.).
learningOutcomes: Open and navigate a modern AI chat or coding assistant
Write a clear, scoped prompt for a real task
Get a usable result (text, code, or plan) on screen
Critique and fix weak AI output instead of accepting it blindly
Explain the task, the prompt, and the outcome in plain language

artifact.initialState: no AI session, no clear task, no result
artifact.finalState: a finished tiny win from AI plus a teach-back of how they got it
artifact.previewIfNoProgress: No AI win yet — let's get one on screen

goals.title: Open your AI
goals.goal: Have a real AI tool open and ready — Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Cursor, or similar.
goals.outcome: An AI chat or AI coding tool is open and recognizable on screen.
goals.coachAsk: Help me open an AI tool I can practice with. I'm learning AI fluency from zero if needed. Point at what to click. Claude (claude.ai), ChatGPT, Gemini, or Cursor are all fine — pick whatever is easiest on this Mac. Don't assume I know the names.
goals.doneWhen: An AI chat website or AI coding app is open and clearly visible on screen.
tips: Browser chat apps are perfect for this path
Cursor or another AI IDE is fine if they already use one
If they're logged out, help them get to a usable screen first

concepts: what an AI chat is (you type, it writes back)
common tools: Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Cursor
why practice on the real tool beats watching a demo
commonMistakes: opening a marketing homepage instead of the actual chat
getting stuck on signup walls — pick the tool that's already available
thinking they need to install everything before starting
successExamples: Claude or ChatGPT chat box is visible and ready to type
Cursor is open with a chat or agent panel ready
teachingContext.whyItMatters: You can't get fluent with a tool that isn't open. Muscle memory starts on the real UI.
teachingContext.teachBackPrompt: which AI tool are we using, and what is it for in one sentence?

goals.title: Quick check: what's a scoped task?
goals.goal: Confirm you can spot a well-scoped AI task before picking your own.
goals.coachAsk: Quick multiple-choice check on task scoping.

interactiveMultipleChoice.question: Which of these is a well-scoped task for AI to help with?
interactiveMultipleChoice.explanation: Specific, small deliverables beat vague goals — that's what makes a task easy to prompt for and easy to know when it's done.

goals.title: Pick a tiny real task
goals.goal: Choose one small, concrete task AI can help with — not 'learn AI' in the abstract.
goals.outcome: They can say a single tiny task in plain language (e.g. tip calculator, email draft, rewrite a paragraph, plan a checklist).
goals.coachAsk: Help me pick one tiny real task to do with AI today. Good options: a tip calculator webpage, a short professional email, a grocery checklist, a rewrite of a messy paragraph, or a 5-step plan for something they care about. Get them to pick ONE. Write it as a clear one-liner.
goals.doneWhen: The learner has stated one concrete tiny task in plain language (spoken, typed, or visible on screen).
tips: One feature or one short deliverable only
If they aim too big, shrink it until it fits in 10 minutes

concepts: AI is a collaborator for a job-to-be-done
tiny wins build fluency faster than mega-projects
commonMistakes: asking for 'an app' with ten features
tasks that require private company data they shouldn't paste
successExamples: Make a single HTML tip calculator
Draft a polite follow-up email under 120 words
Turn my bullet notes into a 5-item checklist
teachingContext.whyItMatters: Clear tasks make prompts better and make 'done' obvious.
teachingContext.teachBackPrompt: what is the one tiny task you're going to get AI to help with?

goals.title: Write a clear prompt
goals.goal: Send one clear prompt: role or context, task, constraints, and what good looks like.
goals.outcome: A clear prompt is visible as typed or sent in the AI tool.
goals.coachAsk: Help me write and send one clear prompt for the tiny task we picked. Explain what a prompt is if needed — it's just the message you type. Coach them to include: what they want, any constraints (length, language, format), and what 'good' looks like. Point at where to type and how to send. Don't write the whole prompt for them unless they ask — coach them to type it.
goals.doneWhen: A clear, scoped prompt for the chosen task is visible as typed or already sent in the AI chat.
tips: One task per prompt to start

commonMistakes: pasting secrets or private data they shouldn't share
successExamples: Write a single HTML file for a tip calculator with bill, tip %, and total. Keep it simple.
Draft a 3-sentence follow-up email to a hiring manager, friendly and short.
teachingContext.whyItMatters: Prompt quality is the core AI fluency skill for almost every role.
teachingContext.teachBackPrompt: what makes a prompt clear enough that AI can actually help?

goals.title: Quick check: the right word
goals.goal: Confirm you know the term for what you just wrote.

interactiveFillInBlank.prompt: Fill in the blank: the message you type to tell the AI what you want is called a ___.
interactiveFillInBlank.explanation: That's the term — prompt. You'll hear it constantly once you start using AI tools seriously.

goals.title: Get a usable result
goals.goal: Have a usable AI result on screen for the task — draft, code, plan, or checklist.
goals.outcome: Visible AI output that addresses the tiny task (even if imperfect).
goals.coachAsk: Help me get a usable result from the AI for our tiny task. If they already sent the prompt, look at the response with them. If nothing useful came back, help them re-prompt once. Point at the output. If the task was code, help them see it clearly. Don't skip ahead to polishing yet — we just need a real result on screen.
goals.doneWhen: AI-generated content that addresses the chosen task is clearly visible on screen.
tips: Imperfect is fine — we fix next
If the model refused or failed, re-scope the prompt
Scroll so the key result is visible for verification

concepts: AI returns a first draft, not magic truth
seeing the result is required before judging quality
commonMistakes: stopping after a vague or empty reply
accepting the first word without reading
hiding the result so nothing can be checked
successExamples: HTML or code block for the tip calculator is on screen
Email draft is fully visible in the chat
Checklist or plan is readable end to end
teachingContext.whyItMatters: Fluency means producing something real, not talking about AI in theory.
teachingContext.teachBackPrompt: what did the AI give you, in one sentence?

goals.title: Critique and fix
goals.goal: Improve the result once: spot a flaw, re-prompt or edit, and get a better version.
goals.outcome: A second, improved version is on screen, or a clear edit they made themselves.
goals.coachAsk: Help me critique the AI output and improve it once. Look at the screen together. Point out one real issue (too vague, wrong tone, missing piece, bug). Help them either edit it themselves or send a short follow-up prompt to fix that one issue. Celebrate the better version.
goals.doneWhen: An improved second version of the result is visible, or a clear manual edit fixed a real issue.
tips: Follow-up prompts can say: keep everything else, change only X
It's OK to edit the output by hand — that's still fluency

concepts: AI is wrong often — critique is a skill
commonMistakes: rewriting everything instead of one targeted fix
not verifying code or facts when it matters
successExamples: Follow-up: make the email shorter and less formal
They fixed a bug in the HTML and refreshed the page
Checklist now has the missing step they asked for
teachingContext.whyItMatters: Professionals don't accept AI blindly — they steer it.
teachingContext.teachBackPrompt: what was wrong with the first version, and how did you fix it?

goals.title: Quick self-check
goals.goal: Confirm you actually followed the AI fluency loop before wrapping up.
goals.coachAsk: Quick self-check before we wrap up.

goals.title: Explain the win
goals.goal: Explain in plain words: the task, the prompt approach, the result, and one thing they'd do next time.
goals.outcome: They can teach back the loop without reading the chat history word-for-word.
goals.coachAsk: Do a short teach-back. Ask them to explain in their own words: (1) what task they chose, (2) how they prompted, (3) what they got, (4) how they improved it, (5) one thing they'd try next time at work. Use [INFO] and [TODO]. Keep it warm and short — this is the AI fluency finish line.
goals.doneWhen: The learner has explained the task, how they used AI, and the outcome in their own words (voice or text).
tips: If they blank, scaffold with chips: task / prompt / fix
Tie it back to their real job if they mention one

concepts: protégé effect — teaching locks in skill
AI fluency = task → prompt → result → critique
this loop transfers to any role
commonMistakes: reading the chat aloud instead of explaining
skipping the critique step in the story
thinking fluency means memorizing tool names only
successExamples: I needed a short email, I asked for 3 sentences and a friendly tone, then shortened it
I asked for a tip calculator, ran it, fixed the percent math with a follow-up
teachingContext.whyItMatters: If you can teach the loop, you can reuse it on every new tool at work.
teachingContext.teachBackPrompt: walk me through your AI win like you're teaching a coworker
